# The Saturday Market at Port Velling

Port Velling is a small fishing town on a cold northern bay. Every Saturday
from April to October, the old rope warehouse on Quay Street becomes a market.
This guide was written by Marta Oyelaran, who has run the honey stall there
for eleven years.

## Getting there

Most visitors arrive on the 8:15 ferry from Brannock Island, which docks next
to the lighthouse. Others take the coastal bus, route 42, from the city of
Hollis. Parking is limited to the field behind St. Agnes Church, and the
harbourmaster, Desmond Achterberg, closes the quay to cars at nine o'clock.

## The stalls

The fish stall is run by the Kowalczyk brothers, Piotr and Janek. They sell
mackerel, herring, cod and, in late summer, a few crates of langoustines. Next
to them, Ada Fenwick sells smoked eel and pickled samphire from her family
smokehouse in Dunmere.

The bakery stall belongs to Luis Carvalho. His rye loaves sell out by ten, but
he also bakes cardamom buns, oat biscuits and a dense fruit loaf he calls
"harbour brick". Children queue for his cinnamon knots.

Marta's own stall sells heather honey, clover honey and beeswax candles. In
September she brings a small batch of buckwheat honey, which is dark and
bitter, and which regulars buy before it is even unpacked.

Further in, there is a knife grinder named Tobias Lind, a woman who repairs
fishing nets, a seller of second-hand maps and sea charts, and a stall of
hand-knitted jumpers dyed with onion skins, madder root and woad.

## Food and music

At noon, the Velling Brass Band plays on the loading dock. Their usual pieces
are "The Herring Run", "Lantern Bay" and a slow waltz called "Margit". The tea
tent, run by the Women's Lifeboat Guild, serves strong black tea, lemon cake
and crab sandwiches. All money from the tea tent goes to the lifeboat station.

## Odd traditions

On the last Saturday of the season, the market holds the Gull Race, in which
wooden gulls are floated from the slipway and the first to reach the red buoy
wins a jar of honey. The record holder is a retired teacher named Edith Prow,
who has won six times. The market also keeps a brass bell, salvaged from a
wrecked schooner called the Corrie Dawn, which is rung once to open the market
and twice to close it.

## Practical notes

Cash is preferred, although the bakery and the honey stall accept cards. Dogs
are welcome outside but not in the tea tent. Toilets are at the ferry terminal.
If it rains, the brass band moves inside next to the map seller, and the Gull
Race is postponed rather than cancelled.
